course: Daily Bread Sales: Bakery Production System

lessons.title: Introduction and Why It Matters
lessons.body: A business plan is your bakery's roadmap. Without it, you are baking blindly. In Africa's daily bread market, competition is fierce. A plan helps you buy flour at the best price, set a profit margin, and know when to expand. For example, if you sell 200 loaves a day at 10 birr each, that's 2,000 birr daily. But your costsâflour, yeast, salt, firewood, labourâmight be 1,600 birr. That leaves 400 birr profit. Without a plan, you might not notice that your profit is shrinking because flour prices rose. The five stages of a business plan are: 1) Market Research, 2) Production Plan, 3) Financial Plan, 4) Marketing Plan, and 5) Action Plan. Each stage builds on the last. Many small bakeries fail because they skip research and jump to baking. They don't know their customers or competitors. A plan forces you to answer: Who will buy? At what price? How many? What will it cost? Where will you sell? When will you break even? In Kenya, a woman named Grace started a bakery with no plan. She baked 100 loaves daily but sold only 60. The rest went stale. After writing a simple plan, she reduced to 70 loaves, added mandazi, and increased profit by 30%. Your plan doesn't need to be fancy. A notebook and pen are enough. But you must write it down. This module will guide you through each stage with practical steps, local examples, and tools you can use today. By the end, you will have a one-page business plan ready to guide your daily bread sales.

lessons.title: Tools and Materials
lessons.body: To create a business plan, you don't need a computer. A simple exercise book, a pen, and a calculator (or your phone) will do. But you also need information. Gather these tools: 1) A notebook for your plan. 2) A separate notebook for daily records (sales, expenses). 3) A measuring tape to check your workspace. 4) A clock or watch to time baking. 5) A list of suppliers with prices. 6) A map of your area showing potential customers (schools, offices, bus stops). For market research, you need to talk to people. Prepare a simple survey: ask 20 people how many loaves they buy daily, what price they pay, and where they buy. Use tally marks. For financial planning, you need current prices: a bag of flour (50 kg) costs about 1,800 birr in Ethiopia, 2,500 shillings in Kenya, or 1,200 naira in Nigeria. Yeast, salt, sugar, and fuel also have prices. Write them down. For production planning, measure your oven capacity. How many loaves can you bake per hour? A traditional clay oven might bake 30 loaves per batch. A gas oven might do 60. You also need a scale to weigh dough for consistent loaf sizes. For marketing, you need samples to give potential customers. For the action plan, you need a calendar to set deadlines. All these tools are inexpensive and locally available. If you have a smartphone, you can use free apps like Google Sheets or a simple notes app. But paper works just as well. The key is to record everything. Without records, your plan is just guesses. With records, you can see what works and adjust.

lessons.title: Step by Step Method
lessons.body: Follow these five stages to build your business plan. Stage 1: Market Research. Spend one week talking to 30 potential customers. Ask: How many loaves do you buy daily? What price? Where? Note their answers. Also visit 5 competitors. What do they sell? At what price? What are their busy hours? Write a summary: 'I will sell 150 loaves daily at 10 birr each to workers and students in my area.' Stage 2: Production Plan. Decide how many loaves to bake daily. If demand is 150, bake 160 to allow for spoilage. Calculate ingredients: For 160 loaves, you need 50 kg flour, 1 kg yeast, 1 kg salt, 2 kg sugar, and fuel. Write the steps: mix, knead, proof, bake. Time each step. For example, mixing 30 minutes, kneading 45 minutes, proofing 1 hour, baking 30 minutes. Plan your schedule: start at 4 AM to finish by 7 AM. Stage 3: Financial Plan. List startup costs: oven (5,000 birr), mixer (2,000), trays (500), initial ingredients (3,000), rent (1,500 per month). Total: 12,000 birr. Then monthly costs: flour (1,800 x 30 = 54,000), yeast (200 x 30 = 6,000), fuel (300 x 30 = 9,000), labour (2,000), rent (1,500). Total monthly cost: 72,500 birr. Revenue: 160 loaves x 10 birr x 30 days = 48,000 birr. Waitâthat's a loss! So you must adjust: either raise price, reduce costs, or sell more. Maybe sell at 12 birr: 160 x 12 x 30 = 57,600. Still loss. So you need to sell 200 loaves at 12 birr: 72,000. Close. Add mandazi or cakes to increase revenue. This is why the financial plan is crucial. Stage 4: Marketing Plan. How will customers know you? Use signs, word of mouth, free samples. Offer a loyalty card: buy 10 loaves, get 1 free. Partner with local tea shops. Stage 5: Action Plan. Set deadlines: by next Monday, buy flour. By Wednesday, test recipes. By Friday, start selling. Review weekly and adjust.

lessons.title: Common Mistakes and Fixes
lessons.body: Mistake 1: No market research. Many bakers assume they know what customers want. Fix: Talk to at least 30 people. Ask about price, quantity, and preferences. In Tanzania, a baker made only white bread, but customers wanted brown. He lost sales. After surveying, he added brown bread and sales rose 40%. Mistake 2: Underestimating costs. You forget to include fuel, transport, or spoilage. Fix: Track every expense for one month. Add 10% for unexpected costs. For example, if you think flour costs 1,800 birr, add 200 for transport. Mistake 3: Overestimating sales. You bake 200 loaves but sell 100. Fix: Start small. Bake 50 loaves for one week. If you sell all, increase by 20 next week. In Uganda, a baker baked 300 loaves on day one and lost half to spoilage. He then started with 80 and grew steadily. Mistake 4: Ignoring competition. If three bakeries sell at 8 birr, you cannot sell at 15. Fix: Visit competitors. Note their price, quality, and location. Differentiate: offer fresher bread, longer hours, or delivery. Mistake 5: No record keeping. Without records, you don't know profit. Fix: Use a simple notebook. Write daily sales and expenses. At week's end, subtract expenses from sales. If profit is low, find why. Mistake 6: Mixing personal and business money. Fix: Keep separate tins or accounts. Pay yourself a fixed salary. Mistake 7: Giving up too soon. Many bakeries take 3-6 months to become profitable. Fix: Review your plan monthly. Adjust prices, products, or marketing. Stay committed. Mistake 8: Not adapting. If a new competitor opens, you must respond. Fix: Add valueâoffer sliced bread, home delivery, or bulk discounts. These fixes are simple but require discipline. Write them in your plan as 'What I will do if...' scenarios.

lessons.title: Safety and Best Practice
lessons.body: Safety in a bakery is not just about fire and knives; it's also about food safety and financial safety. For food safety: always wash hands before handling dough. Keep raw dough away from baked bread. Store flour in dry, airtight containers to prevent weevils. Use clean water. Bake bread to an internal temperature of 90Â°C to kill bacteria. Cool bread on racks, not on the floor. For fire safety: keep a bucket of sand or water near the oven. Never leave the oven unattended. Wear oven mitts. Keep children away from hot surfaces. For personal safety: lift heavy flour bags with your legs, not your back. Take breaks to avoid fatigue. For financial safety: keep business money separate from personal money. Use a lockable box or mobile money account. Record every transaction immediately. Don't lend business money to friends. Best practices: 1) Weigh ingredients accurately. Inconsistent loaves lose customers. 2) Maintain a cleaning schedule: sweep, wipe, and sanitise daily. 3) Train your workers on hygiene and safety. 4) Have a backup supplier for flour and yeast. 5) Keep a fire extinguisher if possible. 6) Label containers to avoid mixing salt and sugar. 7) Set aside 10% of profit for emergencies. 8) Review your business plan every three months. 9) Network with other bakers to share tips and bulk-buy ingredients. 10) Comply with local health regulations. In many African countries, you need a food handler's permit. Get it. It builds trust. Safety and best practice protect your health, your customers, and your business. They are not optional; they are part of your daily bread.

lessons.title: Practical Exercise
lessons.body: Now it's time to write your own one-page business plan. Follow these steps and fill in the blanks. Use a notebook. Step 1: Market Research. Talk to 10 people today. Ask: How many loaves do you buy daily? What price? Where? Record answers. Then visit 3 competitors. Note their price, location, and busy hours. Write a sentence: 'I will sell ____ loaves daily at ____ birr each to ____ (customer type) in ____ (location).' Step 2: Production Plan. Decide daily production. If you plan to sell 100 loaves, bake 110. List ingredients for 110 loaves: flour (35 kg), yeast (0.7 kg), salt (0.7 kg), sugar (1.4 kg), fuel (enough). Write your schedule: start time, mixing, kneading, proofing, baking, cooling. Step 3: Financial Plan. Calculate startup costs: oven, mixer, trays, initial ingredients, rent, permits. Total: ____ birr. Calculate monthly costs: flour, yeast, salt, sugar, fuel, labour, rent, transport. Total: ____ birr. Calculate monthly revenue: loaves per day x price x 30. If revenue is less than costs, adjust price or quantity. Aim for at least 20% profit. Step 4: Marketing Plan. List 3 ways to attract customers: e.g., free samples, loyalty card, signboard. Write your unique selling point: 'My bread is ____ (fresher, cheaper, larger).' Step 5: Action Plan. Set deadlines: By ____ (date), buy ingredients. By ____, test recipe. By ____, start selling. By ____, review sales. Write your plan on one page. Keep it where you can see it daily. Review weekly. Adjust as needed. This exercise turns your dream into a concrete plan. Do it now, and you are on your way to a successful daily bread business.

quiz.q: What is the first stage of a business plan?
quiz.explanation: Market research is the foundation because it tells you who will buy and at what price.

quiz.q: Why is a business plan important for a bakery?
options: A) It helps you buy flour at the best price
B) It guarantees you will never fail
C) It replaces the need for record keeping
D) It is required by law in all countries
quiz.explanation: A plan helps you make informed decisions about pricing, costs, and expansion.

quiz.q: How many stages are in the business plan described in this module?
quiz.explanation: The five stages are Market Research, Production Plan, Financial Plan, Marketing Plan, and Action Plan.

quiz.q: What simple tool can you use to write a business plan?
quiz.explanation: A notebook and pen are sufficient; no fancy tools are needed.

quiz.q: What should you include in a market research survey?
options: A) How many loaves people buy daily
quiz.explanation: All these questions help you understand demand and competition.

quiz.q: What is a key tool for financial planning?
options: B) A list of supplier prices
quiz.explanation: Knowing current prices for ingredients and fuel is essential for accurate cost calculations.

quiz.q: Why should you measure your oven capacity?
options: A) To know how many loaves you can bake per hour
B) To decide on the price of bread
D) To choose a marketing strategy
quiz.explanation: Oven capacity determines your daily production limit.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a production plan?
options: A) To decide how many loaves to bake daily
B) To set the selling price
quiz.explanation: The production plan matches baking quantity with expected demand.

quiz.q: In the financial plan example, what was the monthly revenue if selling 160 loaves at 10 birr each for 30 days?
quiz.explanation: 160 loaves x 10 birr x 30 days = 48,000 birr.

quiz.q: What should you do if your financial plan shows a loss?
options: B) Raise price, reduce costs, or sell more
quiz.explanation: Adjusting price, costs, or volume can turn a loss into a profit.

quiz.q: What is a common mistake in business planning?
quiz.explanation: Underestimating costs leads to inaccurate profit projections.

quiz.q: How can you fix overestimating sales?
options: A) Bake as much as possible
B) Start small and increase gradually
quiz.explanation: Starting with a small batch and increasing based on actual sales reduces waste.

quiz.q: Why is record keeping important?
options: A) It helps you know your profit
C) It is required by law
D) It replaces a business plan
quiz.explanation: Records show actual sales and expenses, so you can calculate true profit.

quiz.q: What should you do if a new competitor opens nearby?
options: B) Lower your price to match
C) Add value like delivery or loyalty cards
quiz.explanation: Differentiating your product or service helps retain customers.

quiz.q: What is a best practice for food safety?
options: A) Store flour in open sacks
B) Wash hands before handling dough
C) Cool bread on the floor
quiz.explanation: Handwashing prevents contamination and keeps bread safe.

quiz.q: What internal temperature should bread reach to kill bacteria?
quiz.explanation: Baking to 90Â°C ensures harmful bacteria are destroyed.

quiz.q: What should you keep near the oven for fire safety?
options: A) A bucket of sand or water
quiz.explanation: Both sand/water and a fire extinguisher are recommended for fire safety.

quiz.q: Why should you separate business and personal money?
options: A) To avoid confusion and track profit
B) To hide money from family
quiz.explanation: Separation makes it easier to know if the business is profitable.

quiz.q: What percentage of profit should you set aside for emergencies?
quiz.explanation: Setting aside 10% helps cover unexpected costs.

quiz.q: What is a unique selling point (USP)?
options: A) A feature that makes your bread different from competitors
B) The price of your bread
C) The location of your bakery
D) The number of loaves you bake
quiz.explanation: A USP is what makes customers choose you over others.

quiz.q: In the practical exercise, how many people should you talk to for market research?
quiz.explanation: The exercise suggests talking to 10 people today.

quiz.q: What should you do if you plan to sell 100 loaves?
options: B) Bake 110 to allow for spoilage
quiz.explanation: Baking slightly more than expected sales covers potential spoilage or extra demand.

quiz.q: What is the target profit margin mentioned in the practical exercise?
quiz.explanation: Aim for at least 20% profit to ensure sustainability.

quiz.q: Why is it important to review your business plan regularly?
options: A) To adjust to changes in costs, demand, or competition
B) To keep it looking neat
quiz.explanation: Regular review helps you stay on track and adapt to new conditions.

quiz.q: What is a common mistake when setting prices?
options: B) Pricing too low to attract customers
quiz.explanation: Both ignoring competitors and pricing too low can lead to losses.

quiz.q: What should you do before starting to sell bread?
options: B) Test your recipe and get feedback
quiz.explanation: Testing the recipe ensures quality and customer satisfaction.

quiz.q: What is a good way to attract customers?
quiz.explanation: Free samples allow potential customers to taste your product.

quiz.q: What should you do if you don't have a computer?
options: B) Use a notebook and pen
quiz.explanation: A notebook and pen are perfectly adequate for writing a business plan.

quiz.q: What is the final stage of the business plan?
quiz.explanation: The Action Plan sets deadlines and steps to implement the plan.

quiz.q: Why is it important to set deadlines in your action plan?
options: A) To motivate you to take action
quiz.explanation: Deadlines create urgency and help you achieve goals.
